Further reading, if you're interested in the unprecedented monetary policy currently taking place:

Essentially, excessively low interest rates fuel debt growth (naturally, since acquiring debt is cheaper), which fuels bubbles, which must ultimately bust. The end result is that there must be more monetary stimulus after the bust, creating more debt and another bubble, rinse and repeat forever while the rich get richer and the poor get poorer. Unfortunately it's a vicious cycle because at the end of each bubble there is more debt, and even more reason for aggressive monetary stimulus, further inflating asset prices for those who own them (benefiting guess who--those who own the most assets, i.e. rich people). It has never been more clear than in the recent bust and "recovery" (or, echo bubble). Wages are stagnant, but asset prices are at all-time highs.

Your comments about exchange rates are slightly inaccurate. Although we have been seeing a rising dollar as of late, the causes are more than just the expectation of a tiny 0.25% raise in the target fed funds rate. It's mostly because of the aggressive quantitative easing (read: money printing) by the ECB and BOJ, which the Fed also did but as we all know has tapered and finally stopped, and a deteriorating Canadian economy. Also, the dollar is nowhere near record highs generally, and not even specifically vs. the Yen and Euro. Though with the Euro being a young currency, we are approaching its record low if the downtrend continues.

Essentially the only way we can keep a weak dollar to help our exporters would be to re-enter the currency war with more aggressive monetary policy to match the policy of the ECB and BOJ.
